intro: The Talmud is not only about big ideas. It is also about everyday life. What do you do when you find a lost wallet? How much can a store charge? When should a worker get paid? The rabbis argued about questions like these for hundreds of years.

In this unit you will read rules from the tractate Bava Metzia about finding, buying and working. Then you will read about tzedakah, welcoming guests, visiting the sick and saving a life. Each rule has an argument behind it. Each rule also protects someone, like the owner of a lost thing, a worker or a person who is sick.

By the end you will be able to explain these rules in your own words. You will name where each one is found, like Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1. You will also be able to say how Jews have read these rules, and how different readers sometimes disagree.
bigQuestion: How do the Talmud's rules about everyday life try to be both fair and kind?

test.q: What does the name Bava Metzia mean?
test.why: Bava Metzia means 'the middle gate.' It sits between Bava Kamma, the first gate, and Bava Batra, the last gate.

test.q: In Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1, two people hold one garment. What does each one say?
choices: It belongs to a third person
I found it, and all of it is mine
test.why: In the Mishnah each person says, 'I found it, all of it is mine.' The Mishnah then has them swear and split it.

test.q: How does an owner usually prove a lost thing is theirs?
choices: By asking a judge to guess
By describing a siman, a sign on it
test.why: The Mishnah in Bava Metzia says the owner describes a siman, a sign, so the finder knows whom to give it to.

choices: Giving up hope of getting a lost thing back
test.why: Ye'ush means the owner has given up hope. The Gemara in Bava Metzia 21b argues about when that counts.

test.q: Abaye and Rava argue in Bava Metzia 21b. What is their question?
choices: Does giving up count if the owner does not yet know the thing is lost?
How many guests came to Abraham?
test.why: They argue about giving up without knowing. Abaye says it does not count; Rava says it does.

test.q: Which verse does the Torah give about honest scales?
test.why: Leviticus 19:36 says, 'Just balances, just weights ... shall ye have.' The rabbis built rules for fair selling on it.

choices: Cheating on a price, or hurting with words
test.why: Ona'ah means wronging someone. The Mishnah uses it for overcharging and also for hurtful words.

test.q: When does Deuteronomy 24:15 say a worker should be paid?
choices: At the end of the year
When the boss feels like it
On the same day, before the sun goes down
test.why: Deuteronomy 24:15 says, 'In the same day thou shalt give him his hire.' The Talmud builds its rules for paying workers on it.

test.q: Why do many teachers say tzedakah is more than charity?
choices: The word comes from the Hebrew for justice
It is only for rich people
It means a gift of food only
It is a kind of prayer
test.why: Tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice. Rabbinic tradition treats giving as something fair and expected, even from the poor.

test.q: According to Ketubot 50a, what did the rabbis at Usha say about giving?
choices: Do not give more than a fifth
test.why: The Gemara in Ketubot 50a reports a ruling at Usha: do not give more than a fifth, so you do not become poor yourself.

test.q: Which thinker listed eight levels of giving?
test.why: Maimonides lists eight levels in his Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor, chapter 10.

test.q: In Nedarim 40a, what did Rabbi Akiva do for his sick student?
choices: He visited him and cleaned his floor
test.why: Nedarim 40a says Rabbi Akiva visited, swept and sprinkled the floor, and the student said, 'You have given me life.'
Pikuach nefesh means saving a life. In Jewish law as the Talmud develops it, it comes before almost every other rule, even Shabbat.

test.q: The rabbis read Leviticus 18:5, 'he shall live by them.' What did they learn from it?
choices: The rules should be kept only by rabbis
The rules are meant for living, so saving a life comes first
test.why: The Gemara (Yoma 85b) reads 'live by them' to mean one should not die because of them, so saving a life comes first.

test.q: Which text says that saving one life is like saving a whole world?
test.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches that the first human was created alone, so one life is counted like a whole world.

write.prompt: How does the Talmud try to be both fair and kind in everyday life? Pick two or three texts from this unit, such as Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1, Deuteronomy 24:15, Nedarim 40a or Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. For each one, tell what the text says, whom the rule protects, and how the rabbis or later readers explained it.
tips: Name each text you use, with its tractate and page or its book and verse.
Say who is speaking: 'the Mishnah says', 'Rava says', 'Maimonides explains'.
Tell whom each rule protects: the owner, the worker, the poor, the sick.
Use words from the unit, like siman, ona'ah, tzedakah and pikuach nefesh.
If readers disagree, tell both sides without picking a winner.

title: Fair and Kind: Talmud in Everyday Life

chapters.title: Lost and Found, Honest Weights, Fair Wages
chapters.bigQuestion: How does the Talmud try to make everyday trades, finds and jobs fair for everyone?

story.title: One Coat, Two Hands
story.kicker: Two students grab the same coat at the same moment, and a very old book has a plan for that.
paragraphs: It was the last day before winter break at a school in Chicago. The lost-and-found box sat by the door. Maya reached in for a blue coat. Jonah reached in at the same second. Both hands closed on the collar. "It's mine," said Maya. "It's mine," said Jonah. Neither one let go.

Ms. Feld did not take a side. She went to her shelf and pulled down a thick book. "This is a tractate of the Talmud called *Bava Metzia*," she said. "The name means 'the middle gate.' It is about things people find, buy, borrow and lend. And it starts with exactly your problem."

She read the first Mishnah in her own words. Two people are holding one coat. Each says, "I found it." Each says, "It is all mine." The rabbis' answer: each one promises they own at least half. Then they split it. Jonah frowned. "Cut the coat?" "No," said Ms. Feld. "Sell it, and share the money. Or share what it is worth."

"But what if only one of us is telling the truth?" asked Maya. Ms. Feld smiled. "The rabbis asked that too. They asked for pages and pages. That is what the Talmud is: a long, careful argument about being fair." Maya and Jonah looked at the coat. Then they both let go and checked the name tag inside.
story.think: Why might splitting the coat be fairer than letting the faster or stronger person keep it?

lessons.title: Three Gates About Fairness
lessons.mainIdea: Bava Metzia, the middle gate, is one of three tractates about damages, property and fair dealing.
reading: The *Mishnah* is the older, shorter part of the Talmud. Rabbinic tradition says Rabbi Judah the Prince arranged it, around 200 CE. It has six big parts called orders. One order is called Nezikin. The word means 'damages.' It is about harm, money, courts and fairness.

Three of its tractates are called gates. A *tractate* is one book of the Mishnah. Bava Kamma is 'the first gate.' Bava Metzia is 'the middle gate.' Bava Batra is 'the last gate.' Long ago they were one very long book. Later they were split into three parts.

Bava Metzia is about everyday things. What do you do with a lost wallet? What is a fair price? When do you pay a worker? The Gemara, the later discussion, asks questions about each rule. This chapter follows those questions.

words.d: the older, shorter core of the Talmud, a set of rulings arranged around 200 CE
one book of the Mishnah or Talmud, about one set of topics
the order of the Mishnah about damages, property, courts and fair dealing

look.title: The Three Gates
look.cite: Mishnah, order Nezikin; chapter counts as printed in standard editions
look.prompt: The three gates have the same number of chapters. What might that tell you about how they were once one book?

check.q: What does the name Bava Metzia mean?
check.why: Bava Metzia means 'the middle gate.' It sits between Bava Kamma, the first gate, and Bava Batra, the last gate.

check.q: Which order of the Mishnah holds the three gates?
check.why: Nezikin means 'damages.' It is the order about harm, money, courts and fair dealing.

check.q: Which of these is a topic of Bava Metzia?
check.why: Bava Metzia is about things people find, buy, borrow and lend. Lost objects are in its second chapter.

lessons.title: Two Hold One Coat
lessons.mainIdea: The tractate opens with two people holding one garment, and the rabbis' first answer is: promise, then share.
reading: The first Mishnah of Bava Metzia is short. Two people are holding one *tallit*, a cloak or coat. One says, "I found it." The other says, "I found it." Each one says the whole thing is theirs. The Mishnah rules that each one takes an *oath*. Each swears they own no less than half. Then they divide it.

Why an oath? The *Gemara* asks this right away. It gives an answer. If people could just grab and claim, some would grab what is not theirs. A serious promise makes a person stop and think. The Gemara then asks more questions. What if one says it is all his, and the other says only half is his? The Mishnah has an answer for that too.

Readers of the Talmud love this opening. Rashi, a teacher in France about 1,000 years ago, explains each word. Later rabbis wrote whole books on this one page. For the course, notice two things. The rule protects both people. And the rabbis keep asking 'but what if?' That is the way the whole Talmud moves.

words.d: a cloak or garment; in the first Mishnah of Bava Metzia, the thing two people both hold
a very serious promise that something is true
the later discussion of the Mishnah, written in Aramaic and Hebrew

look.title: The First Mishnah, in Plain Words
look.text: Two people are holding a garment. One says, 'I found it,' and the other says, 'I found it.' One says, 'All of it is mine,' and the other says, 'All of it is mine.' Each one swears that he owns no less than half of it, and they divide it.
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1, retold in plain words; compare Michael L. Rodkinson, Babylonian Talmud, 1896–1903
look.prompt: Why do you think the rabbis asked for a promise before the two people share the garment?

check.q: In the first Mishnah of Bava Metzia, what do the two people both say?
check.why: Both people say, 'I found it,' and both claim the whole garment. That is what makes the case hard.

check.q: What does the Mishnah tell the two people to do?
choices: Give it to a judge to keep
Take an oath, then divide it
check.why: Each one swears they own at least half, and then they divide the garment's value.

check.q: What does the Gemara do with the Mishnah's rule?
choices: It copies it with no comment
It asks why and adds harder cases
It turns it into a song
check.why: The Gemara asks why an oath is needed and then tests the rule with new 'what if' cases.

lessons.title: Bring It Back
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah tells a finder to return a lost animal or object, and the rabbis built a whole set of rules on that verse.
reading: The rules about lost things start in the Torah. In Deuteronomy, the fifth book, there is a command. If you see your neighbor's ox or sheep wandering, do not look away. Bring it back. The same goes for a coat or anything lost. Jewish tradition calls this *hashavat aveidah*, returning a lost object.

The second chapter of Bava Metzia takes that verse and asks questions. What counts as lost? What if you do not know whose it is? What if it is a live animal that needs feeding? Do you have to pick up something dirty? The rabbis answer each one. The verse says 'do not hide yourself.' So a person may not pretend they did not see.

The Gemara also protects the finder. If returning a thing would cost the finder more than it is worth, the rules change. An old, honored person is not made to carry a heavy sack through the street. The law asks for kindness, but it is a fair kind of kindness.

words.d: returning a lost object; the rabbis' name for the rule in Deuteronomy 22
the fifth book of the Torah; it holds the verses about lost things and paying workers

look.title: The Verse the Rabbis Start From
look.text: Thou shalt not see thy brother's ox or his sheep driven away, and hide thyself from them; thou shalt surely bring them back unto thy brother.
look.prompt: What two things does this verse say not to do, and what one thing does it say to do?

check.q: Which book of the Torah holds the rule about returning a lost ox or sheep?
check.why: Deuteronomy 22:1–3 tells a person to bring back a neighbor's lost animal or object.

check.q: What does 'hide thyself' mean in the verse?
choices: Pretend you did not see it
check.why: The rabbis read 'hide thyself' as looking away and pretending not to see a lost thing.

check.q: Which case shows the Gemara protecting the finder too?
choices: A finder must carry any load, no matter what
An honored elder is not made to carry a heavy sack
check.why: The Gemara says an elder who would never carry such a load is not forced to; the rule is fair to finders also.

lessons.title: A Sign Tells Whose
lessons.mainIdea: A found thing with a sign is announced; a found thing with no sign, like loose coins, belongs to the finder.
reading: How can a finder know who lost a thing? The Mishnah's answer is the *siman*, a sign. A sign is a mark that only the owner would know. A purse with coins in it has a sign. The owner can say how many coins, or what the purse looks like. Fruit in a basket has a sign: the basket.

Some things have no sign. The Mishnah lists them. Scattered coins in the street. Scattered fruit on the road. A baker's loaves, which all look the same. Loose bundles of grain. No one could prove such a thing was theirs. So the Mishnah says the finder may keep it.

When a thing has a sign, the finder must *announce* it. In Temple times there was a special stone in Jerusalem. Finders stood on it and called out what they found. Someone who lost a thing came and gave the sign. If the sign matched, they got it back. The Mishnah says the loser gives the sign. The finder does not tell it first.

words.d: a sign or mark on a lost thing that only its owner would know
to tell people in public that something was found

look.title: Sign or No Sign?
look.text: Here are four things a person might find on the way to school: a backpack with a name inside; three loose quarters on the sidewalk; one apple rolling on the road; a lunchbox with a sticker and a note. Sort them into two groups: things with a sign, and things with no sign.
look.prompt: For each thing, say why it is in its group. Which ones would the Mishnah say to announce?

check.q: What is a siman?
choices: A sign only the owner would know
check.why: A siman is a sign or mark that shows who the owner is, like the number of coins in a purse.

check.q: Which found thing does the Mishnah say the finder may keep?
choices: A purse with coins in it
check.why: Scattered coins have no sign, so no owner could prove they were theirs. The Mishnah lets the finder keep them.

check.q: Who gives the sign, according to the Mishnah?
choices: The finder tells the sign first
The person who lost the thing
Both must say it at once
check.why: The loser describes the sign. If the finder told it first, anyone could repeat it and claim the thing.

lessons.title: When the Owner Gives Up
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara asks whether an owner who gave up hope still owns the lost thing, and Abaye and Rava disagree.
reading: The rabbis had a word for giving up: *ye'ush*. Say a coin falls into a river. The owner sighs and says, 'It is gone.' Rabbinic tradition holds that the owner has let it go. A finder who pulls it out later may keep it. The owner gave up hope, so the coin is no longer theirs.

Now comes a harder case. What if the owner does not even know the thing is lost yet? Two famous teachers argued about it. They were *Abaye* and *Rava*, who lived in Babylonia around 300 to 350 CE. Abaye said: no. The owner has not given up, because they do not know. Rava said: the owner would give up if they knew. So it counts already.

The Gemara records both views. Later tradition follows Abaye here. This is one of only six cases where the law follows Abaye over Rava. But the point for us is the way the argument goes. Each side brings proofs. Each side answers the other. Both voices stay on the page.

words.d: giving up hope of getting a lost thing back
a Babylonian rabbi of the 300s CE; his debates with Rava fill the Talmud
a Babylonian rabbi of the 300s CE, Abaye's study partner and rival

look.title: Abaye and Rava on Giving Up
look.text: The Gemara asks about giving up without knowing. Abaye says it does not count: the owner has not given up, because he does not yet know the thing is lost. Rava says it does count: once he knows, he will surely give up, so we treat it as given up now.
look.cite: Bava Metzia 21b, paraphrased; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: Which side would you argue for, and what is one reason the other side might give?

check.q: What does ye'ush mean?
choices: Giving up hope of getting it back
check.why: Ye'ush is the owner giving up hope. After ye'ush, the rabbis hold, the finder may keep the thing.

check.q: Abaye and Rava lived in which place?
check.why: Abaye and Rava taught in Babylonia in the 300s CE. Their debates are all through the Gemara.

check.q: In the case of giving up without knowing, what did Abaye say?
choices: It counts, because the owner will give up later
It does not count, because the owner does not know yet
The coin goes to the court
check.why: Abaye said an owner cannot give up on something they do not know is lost. Rava took the other side.

lessons.title: Just Weights and Measures
lessons.mainIdea: Leviticus commands honest scales, and the Mishnah adds rules for keeping measuring tools clean and true.
reading: Long before there were price tags, people bought by weight. A seller put a stone on one side of a *scale*. Grain or oil went on the other side. A cheating seller could use a light stone or a bent scale. The Torah speaks to this. Leviticus says to keep honest scales, honest weights and honest measures.

The Mishnah turns the verse into daily rules. In Bava Batra, the last gate, it says a seller must clean their measures. Sticky oil or wet flour can stick to a cup. Then the buyer gets less. So a wholesaler cleans the measures once a month. A shopkeeper cleans them twice a week. The scale is wiped after every weighing.

The Gemara adds a strong warning. It says a person may not even keep a false weight in the house. Not to use it, just to have it. Why? A false weight is a temptation. Jewish tradition reads this as a rule about trust. If buyers cannot trust the scale, the whole market breaks.

words.d: a tool with two sides for weighing; a seller uses it to measure out goods
the third book of the Torah; it holds the verse about honest weights

look.title: Honest Scales in the Torah
look.text: Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
look.prompt: An ephah measures dry things and a hin measures liquids. Why might the verse name both?

check.q: Which book of the Torah commands honest weights and measures?
check.why: Leviticus 19:35–36 tells people to keep just balances, weights and measures.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say to clean measuring cups?
choices: So the rabbi can bless them
So sticky leftovers do not shortchange the buyer
check.why: Mishnah Bava Batra 5:10 says sticky flour or oil in a cup means the buyer gets less.

check.q: What does the Gemara say about keeping a false weight at home?
choices: It is fine if you never use it
You may not even keep one
check.why: The Gemara, in Bava Batra 89b, says a person may not keep a false weight at all, because it tempts.

lessons.title: No Overcharging
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah calls charging far too much ona'ah, wronging, and sets a clear line: one-sixth over the price.
reading: Sellers set prices. But the Mishnah says there is a limit. Charging much more than a thing is worth is called *ona'ah*. The word means 'wronging' or 'overreaching.' The Torah says in Leviticus, 'You shall not wrong one another.' Rabbinic tradition reads that as a rule about prices.

How much is too much? The Mishnah gives a number. If the price is off by one-sixth, that is ona'ah. The Mishnah uses coins of its day. A *sela* was worth 24 small coins called ma'ah. Four ma'ah over on a sela is one-sixth. At that point the buyer may ask for the extra back. If it is even more, the buyer may cancel the sale.

The rule cuts both ways. A buyer who pays far too little has wronged the seller. The Mishnah protects the person who did not know the price. Historians point out that markets in the Roman world often had no fixed prices. So this was a real protection. It gave a shopper a way to complain.

words.d: wronging someone, in money or in words; charging far too much is ona'ah
a silver coin in the time of the Mishnah, worth 24 ma'ah

look.title: Coins in the Mishnah's Example
rows: Extra ma'ah on a sela that counts as ona'ah
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3, standard coin values as the Mishnah uses them
look.prompt: Four out of 24 is one-sixth. If a fair price today is 12 dollars, how many extra dollars would be one-sixth?

check.q: What does ona'ah mean?
check.why: Ona'ah means wronging. The Mishnah uses it for unfair prices and, later, for hurtful words.

check.q: How far off must a price be for the Mishnah to call it ona'ah?
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3 sets the line at one-sixth, four ma'ah on a sela of 24.

check.q: Who does the ona'ah rule protect?
check.why: A buyer who is overcharged is wronged, and a seller who is underpaid is wronged too.

lessons.title: Hurting With Words
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah says words can wrong a person as much as money can, and the Gemara says even more.
reading: The same Mishnah chapter takes a surprising turn. After prices, it talks about words. Just as there is ona'ah in buying and selling, it says, there is ona'ah in words. The Mishnah gives examples. Do not ask a seller 'how much is this?' if you have no plan to buy. That raises a hope and drops it.

The Mishnah goes on. If a person has changed their ways, do not say, 'Remember what you used to do.' If someone joined the Jewish people from another family, do not bring up their past. Those words hurt. The Gemara adds that shaming a person in public is very serious. It compares the face going pale to a kind of bloodshed.

Then the Gemara compares the two kinds of wronging. Which is worse, money or words? It says words are worse. Why? Money can be given back. A hurtful word cannot be taken back. The Talmud does not just care about fair prices. It cares about a person's *dignity*, their sense of worth.

words.d: wronging with words; hurting someone with what you say
a person's worth and self-respect

look.title: Money or Words?
look.text: Two things happened at the school store. First, Sam was charged two dollars too much for a notebook. Second, a classmate laughed at Sam in front of the line and said, 'You can't even count money.' The Gemara in Bava Metzia says one of these is worse than the other.
look.prompt: Which one does the Gemara say is worse, and what reason does it give? Do you agree?

check.q: Which of these is an example of ona'at devarim from the Mishnah?
choices: Asking a price with no plan to buy
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 says asking 'how much?' with no plan to buy is wronging with words.

check.q: Why does the Gemara say wronging with words is worse than with money?
choices: Money can be given back, but words cannot
check.why: Bava Metzia 58b says money can be returned, but a hurtful word cannot be taken back.

check.q: What does the Gemara compare public shaming to?
check.why: The Gemara notes the face going pale and treats public shaming as very close to shedding blood.

lessons.title: Pay Before the Sun Sets
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says pay a hired worker the same day, and the Mishnah spells out when day and night workers are paid.
reading: Many people in the time of the Mishnah worked by the day. A farmer hired helpers for the harvest. A builder hired carriers. Such a worker needed the money that night to buy food. The Torah knew this. Deuteronomy says: pay him the same day, before the sun goes down, for he is poor and counts on it.

The Mishnah in Bava Metzia makes it exact. A worker hired for the day is paid any time that night. A worker hired for the night is paid any time the next day. A worker hired by the week or the month is paid when the job ends. If the employer holds back pay past that time, the Mishnah says he breaks a Torah rule.

The Mishnah also protects the *employer*, the person who hires. If the worker never asked for pay, the employer has not broken the rule. If the employer handed the pay to a shopkeeper to give the worker, he is not to blame. The rule is not meant to trap anyone. It is meant to get a poor worker fed tonight.

words.d: a person paid by the day, night, week or month for their labor
the person who hires and pays a worker

look.title: The Same Day
look.text: In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD and it be sin in thee.
look.prompt: What reason does the verse give for paying the same day? Who is the verse worried about?

check.q: When must a worker hired for the day be paid, says the Mishnah?
choices: Only at the end of the month
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 9:11 says a day worker collects any time during the following night.

check.q: What reason does Deuteronomy 24:15 give for same-day pay?
choices: The worker is poor and counts on it
check.why: The verse says the worker is poor and sets his heart on the pay, so it must not wait.

check.q: When is an employer NOT to blame for late pay, says the Mishnah?
choices: When the worker did not ask for it
check.why: The Mishnah says if the worker never asked, the employer has not broken the rule of same-day pay.

lessons.title: The Broken Barrels
lessons.mainIdea: A story in Bava Metzia shows a rabbi telling an employer to go beyond the strict law and treat his workers with mercy.
reading: The Gemara tells a story. A man named Rabbah bar bar Chanan hired porters to move barrels of wine. They dropped the barrels, and the wine spilled. He was angry. He took their cloaks as payment for the loss. The porters went to Rav, the great teacher of Babylonia. Rav told the man: give back the cloaks.

The man asked, 'Is that the law?' Rav quoted a verse from Proverbs: 'that you may walk in the way of good men.' He gave back the cloaks. Then the porters said, 'We are poor. We worked all day. We have nothing to eat.' Rav said: pay them their wages. The man asked again, 'Is that the law?' Rav quoted the rest of the verse: 'and keep the paths of the righteous.'

Readers have argued about this story for centuries. Some say Rav found a real rule here. Others say Rav was asking a scholar to go beyond the rule. Jewish tradition has a name for that: *lifnim mishurat hadin*, inside the line of the law. This chapter began with an argument over a coat. It ends with mercy for hungry workers. The Talmud holds both.

words.d: a leading rabbi who brought Mishnah study to Babylonia in the 200s CE
going beyond the strict letter of the law to do what is kind
a worker who carries heavy loads for pay

look.title: Two Ways to Read Rav
look.text: Reading one: Rav was stating the law. Porters who drop a barrel by accident do not owe for it, so the man had to return the cloaks and pay. Reading two: Rav was asking for more than the law. The man was a scholar, and Rav wanted him to act with extra kindness. Both readings come from the same page, Bava Metzia 83a.
look.prompt: Which reading fits the man's question, 'Is that the law?' better? What clue in the story do you use?

check.q: What did Rabbah bar bar Chanan take from the porters?
check.why: After the wine spilled, he took the porters' cloaks. Rav told him to give them back.

check.q: Which book did Rav quote to the employer?
check.why: Rav quoted Proverbs 2:20, 'that thou mayest walk in the way of good men.'

check.q: What does lifnim mishurat hadin mean?
choices: Going beyond the strict law to be kind
check.why: Lifnim mishurat hadin means acting inside, or beyond, the line the law draws, out of kindness.

review.q: What does Bava Metzia mean, and what is it about?
choices: 'The middle gate'; things people find, buy, borrow and lend
review.why: Bava Metzia is 'the middle gate,' the tractate about everyday dealings: finds, sales, loans and wages.

review.q: In the coat case, what happens after the two people take an oath?
review.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1: each swears to at least half, and they divide it.

review.q: A finder picks up a purse with seven coins inside. What does the Mishnah say to do?
choices: Keep it, since coins have no sign
Announce it, since the purse and count are a sign
review.why: Money in a purse has a sign, the purse and the number. Things with a sign must be announced.

review.q: Who argued that giving up without knowing does not count?
review.why: Abaye said an owner who does not know the thing is lost has not given up. Rava disagreed.

review.q: Which verse do the rabbis use for honest scales?
review.why: Leviticus 19:36 commands just balances, just weights and just measures.

review.q: A seller charges one-sixth more than a fair price. What does the Mishnah call this?
review.why: Overcharging by one-sixth is ona'ah, wronging, in Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:3.

review.q: Why does Deuteronomy say to pay a worker before sunset?
choices: Because the worker is poor and counts on the pay
Because coins are hard to see in the dark
review.why: Deuteronomy 24:15 says the worker is poor and sets his heart on the wages.

review.q: In the story of the broken barrels, what did Rav tell the employer to do?
choices: Return the cloaks and pay the porters
review.why: Bava Metzia 83a: Rav told him to give back the cloaks and then to pay the hungry porters.

chapters.title: Tzedakah, Guests and Saving a Life
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the rabbis of the Talmud say a person owes to the poor, the guest, the sick and the person in danger?

story.title: The Radio on Shabbat
story.kicker: It is Saturday morning, a day of rest, and a radio crackles: someone needs help right now.
paragraphs: Saturday morning in a Chicago neighborhood. No cars in the driveway. Uncle Ari's family walks to synagogue on *Shabbat*, the Jewish day of rest. They do not drive. They do not turn on lights. Eight-year-old Noa likes the quiet. Then a small radio on Uncle Ari's belt crackles. A voice says an address. Someone has fallen and cannot breathe well.

Uncle Ari runs. He jumps into a white ambulance parked on the street and drives off. Noa stares. "Isn't it Shabbat?" she asks her mother. "You told me we never drive on Shabbat." Her mother nods. "We don't. Unless a life is in danger. Then the rule changes."

Later, Uncle Ari comes home. The person is at the hospital and will be fine. Noa still has her question. Uncle Ari pulls a book off the shelf. It is a tractate of the Talmud called Yoma. "Long ago," he says, "the rabbis asked your question. What if a wall falls on someone on Shabbat? Do you dig, or do you wait for sunset?"

"You dig," Noa says. "Right," says Uncle Ari. "The rabbis said you dig. Even if you are not sure anyone is under there. Even if it might be too late. They had a name for it: *pikuach nefesh*, saving a life. A rabbi named Shmuel said the Torah's rules are for living by, not for dying by." Noa thinks about the quiet morning and the loud radio. Both, she decides, are part of the same day.
story.think: Why do you think the rabbis said to dig even when you are not sure someone is trapped?

lessons.title: Tzedakah Means Justice
lessons.mainIdea: In Jewish tradition, giving to the poor is called tzedakah, from the word for justice, because the poor have a right to it.
reading: In English, giving to the poor is called charity. The word comes from a Latin word for love. The Hebrew word is different. *Tzedakah* comes from *tzedek*, which means justice. In Jewish tradition, giving to the poor is not only a kind feeling. It is something the poor are owed. It is a matter of fairness.

The Torah sets this up. In Leviticus, a farmer must leave the corners of the field for the poor. That is called *pe'ah*, the corner. Dropped grain stays on the ground for them too. In Deuteronomy, a person must 'open your hand' to a poor neighbor. The Mishnah has a whole tractate called Pe'ah about these rules.

The Mishnah's first lines in Pe'ah are famous. They list things that have no set limit. One is the corner of the field. Another is acts of kindness. Another is study of Torah. Jewish readers have taken this to mean that giving has no top. There is a least amount, the rabbis said, but no most.

words.d: giving to the poor; the word comes from tzedek, justice
the corner of a field left unharvested for the poor; also a tractate of the Mishnah
justice; fairness

look.title: Open Your Hand
look.text: The Torah says that if there is a poor person among you, you must not harden your heart or shut your hand against him. You must open your hand and lend him enough for whatever he needs.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 15:7–8, paraphrased from the JPS Tanakh, 1917
look.prompt: The verse uses the words 'heart' and 'hand.' What is the difference between hardening a heart and shutting a hand?

check.q: What Hebrew word is tzedakah built from?
check.why: Tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice. The idea is that the poor are owed help, not just given it.

check.q: What is pe'ah?
choices: The corner of a field left for the poor
check.why: Pe'ah is the corner of the field the Torah tells farmers to leave for the poor; Mishnah Pe'ah is named for it.

check.q: What does the first Mishnah of Pe'ah say about acts of kindness?
choices: They must be done once a year
check.why: Mishnah Pe'ah 1:1 lists acts of kindness among the things that have no fixed measure.

lessons.title: Everyone Gives
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says even a poor person who lives on tzedakah gives tzedakah, and it sets a floor and a ceiling for giving.
reading: Who has to give? The Gemara in tractate Gittin gives a surprising answer. Even a poor person who is fed by tzedakah must give tzedakah. Why? Because giving is part of being a person, not a thing only rich people do. A small gift from a poor person counts fully. This is a well-known teaching in Jewish life today.

How much? Jewish custom, based on the Torah's tithe, is about a tenth of what you earn. The rabbis also set a top. At a meeting in a town called Usha, about 1,900 years ago, they ruled that a person should not give away more than a fifth. The reason is kind: a person who gives too much may become poor too.

Rabbinic tradition also cares how you give. The Gemara says the poor person's face matters. If someone gives with a sour look, the gift loses its worth. A kind word with the gift counts as much as the gift. Some Jewish readers today say this is the heart of tzedakah: the dignity of the one who receives.

words.d: a tractate of the Talmud; one page in it teaches that even the poor give tzedakah
a tenth part, set aside as a gift
a town in the Galilee where rabbis met and made rulings after the year 135 CE

look.title: How Much to Give
rows: Coins given out of 100, at a tenth
Coins given out of 100, at a fifth (the most, ruled at Usha)
Coins kept out of 100, after giving a fifth
look.cite: Ketubot 50a on the ruling at Usha; the custom of a tenth from the Torah's tithe
look.prompt: Why might the rabbis set a top amount for giving, not only a least amount?

check.q: According to the Gemara in Gittin, who must give tzedakah?
choices: Even a poor person who lives on tzedakah
check.why: Gittin 7b says even a poor person supported by tzedakah must give some tzedakah.

check.q: What top amount did the rabbis at Usha set for giving?
check.why: Ketubot 50a records the ruling at Usha: do not give away more than a fifth, so you do not become poor yourself.

check.q: What does the Gemara say about giving with a sour face?
check.why: The rabbis taught that how you give matters; a sour look takes away from the gift.

lessons.title: The Secret Gift
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis prized giving in secret, so the poor are not shamed, and Maimonides put it near the top of his ladder of giving.
reading: The Mishnah describes a room in the Temple in Jerusalem. It was called the chamber of secrets. People who wanted to give slipped money in with no one watching. Poor people from good families took money out the same way. No one saw who gave. No one saw who took. Nobody had to feel shame.

The Gemara tells a story about a rabbi named Mar Ukva. Every day he dropped coins by a poor man's door and hurried away. One day the poor man decided to see who it was. He waited by the door. Mar Ukva and his wife saw him coming and ran. They hid in a hot oven so the man would not see them. Mar Ukva chose burnt feet over shaming a neighbor.

About 800 years ago, a Jewish scholar named *Maimonides* wrote a ladder of giving. It has eight steps. Near the top is giving where neither person knows the other. At the very top is helping a person so they no longer need help at all: a loan, a job, a business partner. Jewish groups still teach this ladder.

words.d: a room in the Temple where gifts were left and taken with no one watching
a Babylonian rabbi in the Gemara who gave to the poor in secret
a Jewish scholar and doctor, c. 1138–1204, who wrote a ladder of eight kinds of giving

look.title: The Ladder of Giving
look.text: Maimonides lists eight levels of giving. The highest is to help a poor person stand on their own, with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so that they need no more help. Next is giving where the giver does not know who receives and the receiver does not know who gave.
look.cite: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–8, paraphrased
look.prompt: Why might helping someone find work rank above handing them money?

check.q: What was the chamber of secrets?
choices: A room where gifts were left and taken unseen
check.why: Mishnah Shekalim 5:6 describes the chamber of secrets, where giving and taking were done without being seen.

check.q: Why did Mar Ukva hide in an oven?
choices: So the poor man would not know who gave
check.why: Ketubot 67b: Mar Ukva ran into an oven rather than let the poor man learn who had been giving to him.

check.q: What is the top step of Maimonides' ladder?
choices: Helping a person so they no longer need help
check.why: Maimonides puts helping someone become self-supporting, through work or a loan, at the top.

lessons.title: Guests Before Everything
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says welcoming guests is even greater than greeting the Divine Presence, and it learns this from Abraham.
reading: In Genesis, Abraham is sitting at his tent door on a hot day. Three strangers appear. He runs to them. He bows. He brings water for their feet. He asks Sarah to bake. He serves the meal himself and stands while they eat. Readers of the Torah have long seen Abraham as the model of *hospitality*, welcoming guests.

The Gemara in tractate Shabbat makes a bold claim from this story. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the *Shekhinah*, the Divine Presence. How does he know? In the story, Abraham seems to be speaking with God when the strangers appear. Yet he turns to greet them first.

This teaching is written on the walls of many Jewish homes and schools. In Pirkei Avot, a sage says, 'Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household.' Jewish families of many kinds, Orthodox, Conservative and Reform, invite guests to Shabbat meals. Many say this page of Talmud is why.

words.d: welcoming guests warmly; in Hebrew, hakhnasat orchim
a rabbinic name for God's presence in the world
'Chapters of the Fathers,' a tractate of short sayings by the rabbis

look.title: Abraham's Guests, by the Numbers
rows: Strangers who came to Abraham's tent (Genesis 18:2)
Measures of fine flour Sarah baked (Genesis 18:6)
Abraham's age just before, at his circumcision (Genesis 17:24)
look.prompt: The Gemara says Abraham was resting after his circumcision. How does his age make his running to the guests more striking?

check.q: Who is the Talmud's model of welcoming guests?
check.why: Shabbat 127a learns hospitality from Abraham running to greet three strangers in Genesis 18.

check.q: What does Rav say welcoming guests is greater than?
check.why: Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Shekhinah, the Divine Presence.

check.q: Which tractate holds the saying 'Let your house be open wide'?
check.why: Pirkei Avot 1:5 records the saying about an open house and the poor as members of the household.

lessons.title: Visiting the Sick
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis treated visiting the sick as a duty, and they told stories to show how much a visit can do.
reading: The Gemara in tractate Nedarim tells a story about Rabbi Akiva. One of his students got sick. No one went to see him. Rabbi Akiva went himself. He swept the floor and tidied the room. The student said, 'Rabbi, you have brought me back to life.' Rabbi Akiva then taught: whoever does not visit the sick, it is as if he sheds blood.

The same page has a saying from Rabbi Acha bar Chanina. Each person who visits takes away one-sixtieth of the illness. Others asked: then sixty visitors would cure anyone? The Gemara answers: only if each one cares as much as the sick person cares. The point is not magic. The point is that visits help.

Why is this a duty? The Gemara in Sotah gives a reason. It says God visited Abraham when he was healing. So people should visit the sick too. Jewish tradition calls this *bikkur cholim*, visiting the sick. Many synagogues in Chicago and everywhere have a bikkur cholim group that visits hospitals.

words.d: visiting the sick; a duty in Jewish tradition
a great teacher in the Land of Israel, c. 50–135 CE
a tractate of the Talmud; its pages 39b–40a discuss visiting the sick

look.title: Rabbi Akiva Sweeps the Floor
look.text: A student of Rabbi Akiva fell ill, and the sages did not visit him. Rabbi Akiva went in to visit him. Because he swept and sprinkled the floor before him, the student lived. He said, 'My teacher, you have given me life.' Rabbi Akiva went out and taught: anyone who does not visit the sick, it is as if he sheds blood.
look.cite: Nedarim 40a, paraphrased; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: What did Rabbi Akiva actually do in the room? Why might such a small thing matter so much?

check.q: What did Rabbi Akiva do when he visited his sick student?
choices: He swept and tidied the room
check.why: Nedarim 40a says Rabbi Akiva swept and sprinkled the floor, and the student said it gave him life.

check.q: What does bikkur cholim mean?
check.why: Bikkur cholim is the Hebrew name for visiting the sick.

check.q: How much of the illness does one visitor take away, says Rabbi Acha bar Chanina?
check.why: Nedarim 39b: one-sixtieth. The Gemara adds that this works only for a visitor who truly cares.

lessons.title: Kindness Bigger Than Money
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says acts of kindness reach further than money, and it extends care to the poor and sick of every people.
reading: The Gemara in Sukkah compares two things. One is tzedakah, giving money. The other is *gemilut chasadim*, acts of kindness. Rabbi Elazar says kindness is greater in three ways. Money helps only the poor; kindness helps rich and poor. Money uses only your hand; kindness uses your whole self. Money helps only the living; kindness can honor the dead.

The Talmud also asks who is owed this care. In tractate Gittin, the rabbis rule that Jews support the poor of other peoples along with the poor of the Jewish people. They visit the sick of other peoples. They bury the dead of other peoples. The reason given is *darkhei shalom*, the ways of peace.

Readers today differ on how far these words reach. Some see them as a practical rule for living side by side. Others see them as a full call to care for every person. The course does not settle that. But notice the move: a rule made for one group is opened to the stranger. The two threads of this course, argument and mercy, meet here.

words.d: acts of kindness done with your own body and time, not only money
'the ways of peace,' a reason the rabbis give for caring for people of other groups

look.title: Three Ways Kindness Is Bigger
look.text: Rabbi Elazar in Sukkah 49b: tzedakah is done with money, kindness with money or with your body; tzedakah goes to the poor, kindness to poor and rich; tzedakah goes to the living, kindness to the living and the dead. Think of one act of kindness that fits each of the three.
look.prompt: Name one act of kindness that uses your body, one for someone who is not poor, and one that honors someone who has died.

check.q: Who does Rabbi Elazar say tzedakah helps, compared with kindness?
choices: Tzedakah helps only the poor; kindness helps rich and poor
Tzedakah helps everyone; kindness helps only the rich
check.why: Sukkah 49b: money reaches only the poor, but acts of kindness reach rich and poor alike.

check.q: What reason does Gittin give for supporting the poor of other peoples?
choices: Darkhei shalom, the ways of peace
check.why: Gittin 61a says these acts are done 'for the ways of peace,' darkhei shalom.

check.q: What does gemilut chasadim mean?
check.why: Gemilut chasadim are acts of kindness done with one's own effort, like visiting or comforting.

lessons.title: Move the Stones
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah in Yoma says that when a life may be in danger, you break Shabbat to save it, even if you are not sure.
reading: *Shabbat* is the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Jewish tradition holds that the Torah forbids work on that day. The Mishnah lists 39 kinds of work. Digging, carrying and lighting a fire are on the list. So what happens if a wall falls on someone on Shabbat?

The Mishnah in tractate Yoma answers. If rubble falls on a person, you clear it away. Even if you are not sure anyone is under it. Even if you are not sure the person is alive. You keep digging until you know. The rabbis called this *pikuach nefesh*, saving a life. It sets aside almost every other rule.

The Gemara asks: how do we know? Several rabbis give proofs. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says, break one Shabbat for him, so he can keep many Shabbatot. Shmuel gives a verse from Leviticus: the rules are given so that a person 'shall live by them.' He adds: and not die by them. The Gemara says Shmuel's proof is the strongest.

words.d: the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night
saving a life; in Jewish law, it sets aside almost every other rule
the tractate about the Day of Atonement; its eighth chapter discusses saving a life

look.title: Live by Them
look.text: Ye shall therefore keep My statutes, and Mine ordinances, which if a man do, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.
look.prompt: Shmuel read 'live by them' as 'and not die by them.' Is that what the words say, or is it a reading he adds? Explain.

check.q: What does the Mishnah in Yoma say to do if rubble falls on someone on Shabbat?
choices: Clear it away, even if you are not sure anyone is there
Only call out to the person
check.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:7: you clear the rubble, even in doubt, because a life may be at stake.

check.q: Which verse does Shmuel use to prove that saving a life comes first?
choices: Proverbs 2:20, the way of good men
check.why: Yoma 85b: Shmuel reads Leviticus 18:5, 'live by them,' as 'and not die by them.'

check.q: What does pikuach nefesh mean?
check.why: Pikuach nefesh means saving a life. Jewish law places it above almost every other rule.

lessons.title: One Life, a Whole World
lessons.mainIdea: A famous Mishnah in Sanhedrin says that whoever saves a single life is counted as if they saved a whole world.
reading: The Mishnah in tractate *Sanhedrin* describes a courtroom. A person is on trial for their life. Before the witnesses speak, the judges warn them. A mistake here cannot be undone. Then the judges explain why one life matters so much. The first human, they say, was created alone.

From that, the Mishnah draws a lesson. Whoever destroys a single life is counted as if they destroyed a whole world. Whoever saves a single life is counted as if they saved a whole world. The Mishnah adds another reason. Since all people come from one person, no one can say, 'My father was greater than yours.'

This line is quoted all over the world today. It is carved on memorials. It appears in films. Scholars note that old handwritten copies say 'a single life.' Some later printed copies say 'a single life of Israel.' Most historians think the shorter words are older. Either way, Jewish readers have used this Mishnah to teach that every person is a world.

words.d: the high court in ancient Jewish tradition; also the tractate about courts and judges
a person who tells a court what they saw
a book copied by hand, before printing

look.title: As If a Whole World
look.text: The Mishnah says the first human was created alone to teach that whoever destroys a single life is counted as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single life is counted as if he saved a whole world.
look.cite: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, paraphrased; compare Michael L. Rodkinson, Babylonian Talmud, 1896–1903
look.prompt: The Mishnah says this to witnesses in a court. Why would judges want witnesses to hear it before they speak?

check.q: In Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, who is being spoken to?
check.why: The Mishnah gives the warning judges say to witnesses before a trial where a life is at stake.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say the first human was created alone?
choices: To teach that one life is like a whole world
check.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 says one person was created to teach that a single life equals a whole world.

check.q: What do scholars say about the words 'a single life' in old handwritten copies?
check.why: Most historians think the shorter reading, 'a single life,' is older than copies that add 'of Israel.'

lessons.title: Rules for Mercy
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis made mercy into clear rules, with a few firm limits, and Jewish communities today live by them.
reading: The Mishnah in Yoma gives more cases. On Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, Jewish tradition holds that adults fast all day. But a sick person who needs food is fed. A pregnant woman who smells food and feels faint is fed. The Mishnah says to listen to doctors. If the sick person says they need food, they are fed even if the doctors disagree.

Are there limits? The Gemara says yes, a very short list. In Sanhedrin, the rabbis say a person may not kill another to save their own life. The Gemara asks a sharp question: who says your blood is redder than his? Later rabbis count only three rules that may never be broken, even to live. Every other rule gives way to life.

Today, Jewish doctors, nurses and volunteer ambulance drivers in many cities answer calls on Shabbat. Orthodox, Conservative and Reform rabbis all teach that this is right. They point to Yoma 85. Rabbinic tradition turned a feeling, mercy, into a rule you can follow at 8 a.m. on a Saturday. That is what this unit has been about.

words.d: the Day of Atonement, a fast day in the Jewish year
to go without food and drink for a set time

look.title: A Feeling Becomes a Rule
look.text: Case one: a girl with a fever on Yom Kippur says she is too weak to fast. Case two: a man's radio calls him to an ambulance on Shabbat. Case three: a boy finds a stranger's wallet with a name inside. For each case, name the rule from this unit that applies and the tractate it comes from.
look.prompt: Which of the three cases is about pikuach nefesh, which is about returning a lost object, and which one could be both?

check.q: What does the Mishnah in Yoma say about a sick person on Yom Kippur?
choices: They are fed if they need food
check.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:5 says a sick person is fed on the advice of experts, and even on their own word if they insist.

check.q: What question does the Gemara ask about killing to save yourself?
choices: Who says your blood is redder?
check.why: Sanhedrin 74a: 'Who says your blood is redder than his?' You may not take a life to save your own.

check.q: Which page do rabbis of many kinds point to for driving an ambulance on Shabbat?
check.why: Yoma 85a–b is the main discussion of pikuach nefesh, saving a life on Shabbat.

review.q: Tzedakah comes from the word for what?
review.why: Tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice. Giving to the poor is treated as something owed.

review.q: Who must give tzedakah, according to Gittin 7b?
choices: Even the poor who receive it
review.why: The Gemara says even a poor person who is supported by tzedakah gives tzedakah.

review.q: What did the chamber of secrets in the Temple make possible?
review.why: Mishnah Shekalim 5:6: gifts went in and out unseen, so no one had to feel shame.

review.q: What is at the top of Maimonides' ladder of giving?
review.why: Maimonides ranks helping someone become self-supporting, through a job or loan, as the highest form.

review.q: From whose story does the Talmud learn that guests come first?
review.why: Shabbat 127a learns hospitality from Abraham running to greet three strangers in Genesis 18.

review.q: What did Rabbi Akiva teach after visiting his sick student?
choices: Whoever does not visit the sick is as if he sheds blood
Sweeping is a kind of work
review.why: Nedarim 40a: Rabbi Akiva taught that not visiting the sick is like shedding blood.

review.q: What does 'darkhei shalom' mean in Gittin 61a?
review.why: Darkhei shalom, the ways of peace, is the reason given for caring for the poor and sick of other peoples.

review.q: Which teaching says a person should break one Shabbat so they can keep many?
review.why: Yoma 85b records Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's reason for saving a life on Shabbat.
